{{Short description|Microbiological population model hypothesis}}
[[File:Lotka Volterra dynamics.svg|thumb|The "Kill the Winner" hypothesis relates to [[Lotka–Volterra equations|Lotka-Volterra]] equations. ]][[File:Viral entry (Endocytosis and lysis).svg|thumb|[[Viral lysis]], which disproportionately targets the "winners" of marine ecosystems. ]]
The '''"Kill the Winner" hypothesis''' ('''KtW''') is an ecological model of population growth involving [[prokaryote]]s, [[virus]]es and [[protozoan]]s that links trophic interactions to [[biogeochemistry]].<ref name="Winter_2010" /> The model is related to the [[Lotka–Volterra equations]]. It assumes that prokaryotes adopt one of two strategies when competing for limited resources: priority is either given to population growth ("winners") or survival ("defenders").<ref name="Winter_2010" /> As "winners" become more abundant and active in their environment, their contact with host-specific viruses (also known as [[phage]]s) increases, making them more susceptible to viral infection and [[lysis]].<ref name="Korytowski_2017" /> Thus, viruses moderate the population size of "winners" and allow multiple species (both "winners" and "defenders") to coexist.<ref name="Våge_2014" /> Current understanding of KtW primarily stems from studies of lytic viruses and their host populations.<ref name="Thingstad-1997" /><ref name="Thingstad-2000" /><ref name="Hennes_1995" />

KtW provides a possible solution to the [[paradox of the plankton]].<ref name="Hutchinson_1961" /> It provides a mechanism for species coexistence despite resource limitations. Some investigations into virus-bacteria interactions in laboratory settings have suggested viruses play a major role in maintaining microbial diversity and provided more evidence in support of KtW.<ref name="De Paepe_2014" /><ref name="Zhong_2023" /><ref name="Suttle_2007" />

Competition specialists, or "winners", are often the fastest growing populations.<ref name="Winter_2010">{{cite journal | vauthors = Winter C, Bouvier T, Weinbauer MG, Thingstad TF | title = Trade-offs between competition and defense specialists among unicellular planktonic organisms: the "killing the winner" hypothesis revisited | journal = Microbiology and Molecular Biology Reviews | volume = 74 | issue = 1 | pages = 42–57 | date = March 2010 | pmid = 20197498 | pmc = 2832346 | doi = 10.1128/MMBR.00034-09 }}</ref> Their abundance and activity increases when they outcompete other species for a shared limiting resource (e.g. phosphate). The resource can exist as a free form or as something that needs to be sequestered from [[biomass]]. Competition specialists (predators, grazers, parasites) are expected to dominate in oligotrophic environments where [[Competition (biology)|competition]] is a large ecological constraint.<ref name="Winter_2010" /> When competition specialists are found at uncharacteristically low abundances in oligotrophic environments, viruses may be responsible for moderating their population size.

Defence specialists invest resources in strategies to avoid viral infection, but these strategies may result in reduced growth. Hence, the "defender" does not increase viral predation.<ref name="Winter_2010" /> Defence specialists are expected to dominate in eutrophic environments where competition pressure is reduced.<ref name="Winter_2010" />

While the KtW model is widely applicable to different trophic levels and complex microbial systems, it has many limitations.<ref name="Winter_2010" /><ref name="Korytowski_2017">{{cite journal | vauthors = Korytowski DA, Smith H | title = Permanence and Stability of a Kill the Winner Model in Marine Ecology | journal = Bulletin of Mathematical Biology | volume = 79 | issue = 5 | pages = 995–1004 | date = May 2017 | pmid = 28349407 | doi = 10.1007/s11538-017-0265-6 | arxiv = 1605.01017 | s2cid = 3959038 }}</ref> The KtW model represents an idealized microbial food web with mathematical parameters that only account for viral predation studied ''in vitro''.<ref name="Winter_2010" /><ref name="Våge_2014" /> Because it assumes environmental conditions are stable, it can only predict population dynamics over a small time frame relative to a microbial community's history. It also fails to account for the fact that a prokaryotic species can be attacked by multiple viruses at once. The KtW model may be modified as other models that assess its limitations (e.g. CKTW) are developed.<ref name="Xue-2017" /><ref name="Marantos_2022" />

== History ==

=== Paradox of the plankton ===

The "Kill the Winner" hypothesis is related to the paradox of the plankton, which is an observation that many planktonic species exist despite having similar resource requirements. This paradox was first noted by [[G. Evelyn Hutchinson|G.E. Hutchinson]] in 1961 in relation to phytoplankton.<ref name="Hutchinson_1961" /> He noticed that many distinct species coexisted despite filling the same niche.<ref name="Hutchinson_1961">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Hutchinson GE |date=1961 |title=The Paradox of the Plankton | jstor = 2458386 |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=95 |issue=882 |pages=137–145 |doi=10.1086/282171 |bibcode=1961ANat...95..137H |s2cid=86353285 }}</ref> In a well-mixed [[Pelagic zone|pelagic]] environment, with conditions being roughly constant, prior biological theories (e.g. the [[competitive exclusion principle]]) suggested one species should eventually dominate.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Hardin G |date=April 1960 |title=The Competitive Exclusion Principle |journal=Science |volume=131 |issue=3409 |pages=1292–1297 |doi=10.1126/science.131.3409.1292|pmid=14399717 |bibcode=1960Sci...131.1292H }}</ref> Selective predation, symbiotic interactions, and variations in environmental conditions over space and time were initially proposed as solutions to the paradox.<ref name="Hutchinson_1961" />

=== Virus-bacteria interactions ===
Early modelling of viral infections in bacterial populations assumed a predator-prey relationship between viruses and bacteria following the Lotka-Volterra equations. Viruses and bacteria were thought to coexist stably in cycles of high and low population.<ref name="Levin_1977">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Levin BR, Stewart FM, Chao L |date=1977 |title=Resource-Limited Growth, Competition, and Predation: A Model and Experimental Studies with Bacteria and Bacteriophage | jstor = 2459975 |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=111 |issue=977 |pages=3–24 |doi=10.1086/283134 |bibcode=1977ANat..111....3L |s2cid=85167289 }}</ref> These theoretical models of virus-bacteria interactions were supported by studies of ''[[Escherichia coli]]'' and [[bacteriophage]]s in laboratory settings.<ref name="Levin_1977" /><ref name="Chao-1977" /> It was also observed that multiple strains of ''E.coli'' could coexist if nutrients were limited and phages were introduced to the culture. Growth-oriented, phage-susceptible ''E.coli'' could coexist stably with slower-growing strains that were more resistant to infection.<ref name="Levin_1977" /><ref name="Chao-1977">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Chao L, Levin BR, Stewart FM |date=1977 |title=A Complex Community in a Simple Habitat: An Experimental Study with Bacteria and Phage | jstor = 1935611 |journal=Ecology |volume=58 |issue=2 |pages=369–378 |doi=10.2307/1935611 |bibcode=1977Ecol...58..369C }}</ref> However, these experiments could not replicate the high diversity, grazing, and environmental conditions of marine ecosystems.

=== "Kill the Winner" ===
The "Kill the Winner" hypothesis was first raised in a 1997 study of theoretical models for marine bacterial populations.<ref name="Thingstad-1997" /> In this study, [[Tron Frede Thingstad|T. Frede Thingstad]] and Risto Lignell found that the total size of a bacterial population was controlled by grazing and that lytic viruses had no impact on bacterial abundance in any of their nutrient-limited models.<ref name="Thingstad-1997">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Thingstad TF, Lignell R |date=July 1997 |title=Theoretical models for the control of bacterial growth rate, abundance, diversity and carbon demand |journal=Aquatic Microbial Ecology |volume=13 |pages=19–27 |doi=10.3354/ame013019 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Instead, viruses promoted diversity by preferentially infecting more abundant and active bacteria. Thingstad later found that bacteria with varying growth rates could coexist stably, with faster-growing bacterial species maintaining a higher abundance of viruses.<ref name="Thingstad-2000">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Thingstad TF |date=September 2000 |title=Elements of a theory for the mechanisms controlling abundance, diversity, and biogeochemical role of lytic bacterial viruses in aquatic systems |journal=Limnology & Oceanography |volume=45 |issue=6 |pages=1320–1328 |doi=10.4319/lo.2000.45.6.1320  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2000LimOc..45.1320T |s2cid=85861373 }}</ref> In this way, viruses can prevent the dominance of one species in any particular niche, which maintains microbial diversity and presents a solution to the paradox of the plankton.<ref name="Hutchinson_1961" /> More recent discoveries of the significant role viruses play in cellular turnover also support the idea that viruses play a major role in maintaining planktonic diversity.<ref name="Suttle_2007" />

=== Support for the "Kill the Winner" hypothesis ===
"Kill the Winner" dynamics are primarily observed in aquatic ecosystems.<ref name="De Paepe_2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = De Paepe M, Leclerc M, Tinsley CR, Petit MA | title = Bacteriophages: an underestimated role in human and animal health? | journal = Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology | volume = 4 | page = 39 | date = 2014-03-28 | pmid = 24734220 | pmc = 3975094 | doi = 10.3389/fcimb.2014.00039 | doi-access = free }}</ref> In these environments, the population dynamics of bacteria and their host-specific viruses are often coupled.<ref name="De Paepe_2014" /> For example, data from [[Lake Constance]] in Germany shows that spikes in bacterial abundance generally lead to spikes in viral infection.<ref name="Hennes_1995">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hennes KP, Simon M | title = Significance of bacteriophages for controlling bacterioplankton growth in a mesotrophic lake | journal = Applied and Environmental Microbiology | volume = 61 | issue = 1 | pages = 333–340 | date = January 1995 | pmid = 16534914 | pmc = 1388335 | doi = 10.1128/aem.61.1.333-340.1995 | bibcode = 1995ApEnM..61..333H }}</ref> Additionally, virus-induced mortality makes up a significant portion of total mortality in bacterial communities, illustrating how tightly viruses control bacterial abundance.<ref name="Hennes_1995" />

In 2023, ribosomal sequencing of coastal seawater samples revealed that abundant slow-growing taxa remain abundant because they are subject to low viral lysis.<ref name="Zhong_2023">{{cite journal | vauthors = Zhong KX, Wirth JF, Chan AM, Suttle CA | title = Mortality by ribosomal sequencing (MoRS) provides a window into taxon-specific cell lysis | journal = The ISME Journal | volume = 17 | issue = 1 | pages = 105–116 | date = January 2023 | pmid = 36209336 | pmc = 9751121 | doi = 10.1038/s41396-022-01327-3  | doi-access = free| bibcode = 2023ISMEJ..17..105Z }}</ref> In contrast, fast-growing taxa are rare because they experience high viral lysis.<ref name="Zhong_2023" /> These observations support the principles of KtW in coastal ecosystems.

Interestingly, the principles of KtW are seldom observed elsewhere.<ref name="De Paepe_2014" /> The microbial community of the human gut, for example, does not appear to follow KtW, as these bacteria are less susceptible to virus-induced mortality.<ref name="De Paepe_2014" /> It is suspected that the gut protects bacteria from infection by providing physical barriers as this environment is only partially liquid.<ref name="De Paepe_2014" />

== Competition and defence specialists ==
In the context of the KtW model, competition specialists are "winners" which grow very quickly relative to other taxa.<ref name="Winter_2010" /><ref name="Våge_2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Våge S, Storesund JE, Giske J, Thingstad TF | title = Optimal defense strategies in an idealized microbial food web under trade-off between competition and defense | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 9 | issue = 7 | article-number = e101415 | date = 2014-07-07 | pmid = 24999739 | pmc = 4084851 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0101415 | veditors = Bertilsson S | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2014PLoSO...9j1415V }}</ref> The mechanism behind KtW describes how competition specialists are controlled by predation by phage, granting the slower-growing "defence specialists" access to the resources.<ref name="Marantos_2022">{{cite journal | vauthors = Marantos A, Mitarai N, Sneppen K | title = From kill the winner to eliminate the winner in open phage-bacteria systems | journal = PLOS Computational Biology | volume = 18 | issue = 8 | article-number = e1010400 | date = August 2022 | pmid = 35939510 | pmc = 9387927 | doi = 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1010400 | veditors = Pascual M | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2022PLSCB..18E0400M }}</ref> Phages therefor allow competition specialists and defence specialists to co-exist despite resource limitations.<ref name="Marantos_2022" />
[[File:Roseobacter_strain_HIMB11.jpg|thumb|241x241px|''[[Roseobacter]]'' strain belonging to family ''[[Rhodobacteraceae]]'']]
''[[Rhodobacteraceae]]'' are a family of bacteria that possess many of the aforementioned qualities of competition specialists. They are fast-growing and tend to exist at low abundances in oligotrophic environments because they are primary targets of viral phages and grazers.<ref name="Parsons_2012">{{cite journal | vauthors = Parsons RJ, Breitbart M, Lomas MW, Carlson CA | title = Ocean time-series reveals recurring seasonal patterns of virioplankton dynamics in the northwestern Sargasso Sea | journal = The ISME Journal | volume = 6 | issue = 2 | pages = 273–284 | date = February 2012 | pmid = 21833038 | pmc = 3260494 | doi = 10.1038/ismej.2011.101 | bibcode = 2012ISMEJ...6..273P }}</ref><ref name="Suttle_2007">{{cite journal | vauthors = Suttle CA | title = Marine viruses--major players in the global ecosystem | journal = Nature Reviews. Microbiology | volume = 5 | issue = 10 | pages = 801–812 | date = October 2007 | pmid = 17853907 | doi = 10.1038/nrmicro1750 | s2cid = 4658457 }}</ref> 
[[File:Pelagibacter.jpg|left|thumb|232x232px|''[[Pelagibacter]]'', a SAR11 bacterium.]]
''[[Pelagibacterales]]'', or the SAR11 clade, include bacteria that dominate the world's oceans.<ref name="Suttle_2007"/> These organisms are slow-growing.<ref name="Parsons_2012" /> Thus, their ability to maintain such high abundances in the marine environment suggests that they are less vulnerable to viral predation.<ref name="Suttle_2007"/> Accordingly, SAR11 is categorized as a defence specialist.<ref name="Parsons_2012" />

=== Respiration rate and size ===
With respect to KtW, the moderating effect of viruses on fast-growing competition specialists impacts interpretations of the metabolic activity of bacterial communities at large.

For example, studies of respiration rate among the marine microbe communities of the Gulf of Maine show that ''[[Rhodobacteraceae]]'' are typically larger than members of the [[SAR11 clade]].<ref name="Munson-McGee_2022">{{cite journal | vauthors = Munson-McGee JH, Lindsay MR, Sintes E, Brown JM, D'Angelo T, Brown J, Lubelczyk LC, Tomko P, Emerson D, Orcutt BN, Poulton NJ, Herndl GJ, Stepanauskas R | display-authors = 6 | title = Decoupling of respiration rates and abundance in marine prokaryoplankton | journal = Nature | volume = 612 | issue = 7941 | pages = 764–770 | date = December 2022 | pmid = 36477536 | pmc = 9771814 | doi = 10.1038/s41586-022-05505-3 | bibcode = 2022Natur.612..764M }}</ref> Smaller cells sizes are generally less metabolically active and more slow-growing.<ref name="Munson-McGee_2022" /> In 2022, researchers suggested that staining methods may not be sensitive enough to measure the low respiration rates of very abundant, but slow-growing and small bacteria, such as those from the [[SAR11 clade]].<ref name="Munson-McGee_2022" /> Such limitations give the impression that only a small fraction of bacteria are metabolically active or alive.<ref name="Munson-McGee_2022" /> While the respiration rates of larger competition specialists are easier to detect, these taxa tend to be rare as per the conditions of KtW, giving the same impression.<ref name="Munson-McGee_2022" /> Together, these constraints contextualize on-going debates around the aliveness of marine bacterial communities. Size effects and KtW make it difficult to quantify the number of aquatic bacteria that are actively growing in the world's oceans.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Zweifel UL, Hagstrom A | title = Total counts of marine bacteria include a large fraction of non-nucleoid-containing bacteria (ghosts) | journal = Applied and Environmental Microbiology | volume = 61 | issue = 6 | pages = 2180–2185 | date = June 1995 | pmid = 16535043 | pmc = 1388461 | doi = 10.1128/aem.61.6.2180-2185.1995 | bibcode = 1995ApEnM..61.2180Z }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | vauthors = Choi JW, Sherr EB, Sherr BF |date=September 1996 |title=Relation between presence-absence of a visible nucleoid and metabolic activity in bacterioplankton cells  |journal=Limnology and Oceanography |language=en |volume=41 |issue=6 |pages=1161–1168 |doi=10.4319/lo.1996.41.6.1161|doi-access=free |bibcode=1996LimOc..41.1161C }}</ref>

== Viruses ==
[[Marine viruses]] have different lifestyles which dictate how they interact with their hosts.<ref name="Record_2016">{{Cite journal | vauthors = Record NR, Talmy D, Våge S |date=2016 |title=Quantifying Tradeoffs for Marine Viruses |journal=Frontiers in Marine Science |volume=3 |page=251 |doi=10.3389/fmars.2016.00251 |bibcode=2016FrMaS...3..251R |issn=2296-7745|doi-access=free }}</ref> When [[Lytic cycle|lytic viruses]] infect their hosts, they cause [[lysis]] or the bursting of cells; alternatively, [[lysogenic viruses]] can integrate into the host genome.<ref name="Record_2016" /> Different environmental conditions such as light, temperature, and nutrients may favour one virus lifestyle over the other.<ref name="Record_2016" /> In general, infections by lytic viruses are higher in productive waters where viruses can easily reproduce.<ref>{{Cite journal | vauthors = Payet JP, Suttle CA |date=March 2013 |title=To kill or not to kill: The balance between lytic and lysogenic viral infection is driven by trophic status |journal=Limnology and Oceanography |language=en |volume=58 |issue=2 |pages=465–474 |doi=10.4319/lo.2013.58.2.0465|s2cid=85900662 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2013LimOc..58..465P }}</ref>
[[File:Cyanophages.png|left|thumb|274x274px|A [[myovirus]] which infects cyanobacterium ''[[Prochlorococcus]]''.]]
KtW indicates that competition specialists and defence specialists are infected by viruses with different life cycles.<ref name="Suttle_2007"/> Fast-growing competition specialists are more likely to be infected by [[r-selected]] or lytic viruses.<ref name="Suttle_2007" /> Following infection, these viruses replicate quickly, rapidly killing their hosts.<ref name="Suttle_2007" /> Through this rapid viral replication, populations of competition specialists are tightly controlled by viral predation.

Slow-growing defence specialists are more likely to be infected by [[K selected|K-selected]] or lysogenic viruses.<ref name="Suttle_2007" /> Rather than quickly replicating and killing their hosts, these viruses inhabit the host cell and remain there until environmental conditions are optimal for viral release.<ref name="Suttle_2007" /> As a result, populations of defence specialists remain stable amidst the threat of viral predation.

== Related hypotheses ==

=== Piggyback-the-Winner (PtW) ===
Unlike KtW, the Piggyback-the-Winner (PtW) hypothesis makes a key distinction between lysogenic and lytic viruses and considers viral life cycles. PtW posits that lysogenic viruses are more abundant than lytic viruses when host density is high.<ref>{{Cite book | vauthors = Knowles B  |title=Piggyback-the-Winner: lytic to temperate switching of viral communities |oclc=957781405}}</ref> Hosts may actively recruit lysogenic viruses, which protect the host from closely related viruses, a phenomenon known as superinfection exclusion.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Silveira CB, Rohwer FL | title = Piggyback-the-Winner in host-associated microbial communities | journal = npj Biofilms and Microbiomes | volume = 2 | issue = 1 | article-number = 16010 | date = 2016-07-06 | pmid = 28721247 | doi = 10.1038/npjbiofilms.2016.10 | s2cid = 23911394 | pmc = 5515262 }}</ref> Abundant hosts are parasitized, rather than killed, and high densities of "winners" are maintained.

=== Coevolving KtW model (CKTW) ===
One problematic assumption of the KtW hypothesis is that predator and prey populations are infinite or very large.<ref name="Xue-2017" /> Given this assumption, the Lotka-Volterra equations would unrealistically imply that neither predators (i.e. viruses) nor prey (i.e. prokaryotes) would go extinct. A 2017 study by Chi Xue and [[Nigel Goldenfeld]] tested the effects of the original KtW model on finite populations.<ref name="Xue-2017">{{cite journal | vauthors = Xue C, Goldenfeld N | title = Coevolution Maintains Diversity in the Stochastic "Kill the Winner" Model | journal = Physical Review Letters | volume = 119 | issue = 26 | article-number = 268101 | date = December 2017 | pmid = 29328693 | doi = 10.1103/physrevlett.119.268101 | s2cid = 38038880 | arxiv = 1706.02666 | bibcode = 2017PhRvL.119z8101X }}</ref> Introducing stochasticity into the KtW model resulted in successive viral and prokaryotic extinctions, showing that species coexistence could not be maintained.<ref name="Xue-2017" /> However, KtW models can be adapted to allow predators and prey to coevolve by mutation. As prey evolve to evade predators and predators evolve to overcome new defences, new mutants are introduced. Thus, Coevolving KtW (CKTW) models allow species diversity to be maintained, even for finite populations.
